Senses.PreferredTarget: the word or saying raised for investigation
Senses.Explanation: In later Chan records, this term names a selected word, question, or saying explicitly assigned or raised for sustained examination. Masters tell people to look at it, investigate it, raise it, take it up, or remember it. Dahui Zonggao says to 'look at a saying' (看箇話頭) and immediately supplies Zhaozhou's question, 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?' (狗子還有佛性也無), answered 'no' (無). The corpus likewise supplies Zhaozhou's cypress tree in the courtyard, Yunmen's dry shit-stick, and other named exchanges after directions to look at a saying. Later records define the term directly. Hanyue Fazang says, 'What is called a saying is one matter or one thing before the eyes' (所謂話頭者，即目前一事一法也), and elsewhere says that this one question gathers all spoken and unspoken words of the worldly and world-transcending, therefore it is called the saying (只者一問，便收盡世出世間一切有言無言等語，故謂之話頭). Ruibai Mingxue says that what is spoken of as the saying is one's own native scenery, distinctly and singly bright, not interrupted by a hair's breadth (所言話頭者，即自己本地風光，歷歷孤明，不可絲毫間斷). A later retrospective reports that only in the Song did talk of looking at sayings and exerting effort arise (直至宋朝，始有看話頭、作工夫之說), and says people were told to take up a saying and look at what principle it was. Jiexian criticizes guarding a dead saying without raising doubt (死守話頭，不起疑情). Current allowlist counts show the range: the headword as 'saying,' 2,575 hits in 297 texts; 'investigate a saying,' 187 in 76; 'look at a saying,' 118 in 46; 'one saying,' 136 in 30; 'one's originally investigated saying,' 89 in 50; 'raise a saying,' 35 in 24; 'take up a saying,' 32 in 24; 'the saying consisting of the word no,' 14 in 12; and 'dead saying,' 40 in 33.
Senses.Note: This is a word or saying in the Chinese record, not the name of a separate object, exercise, mantra, or special category. The sense is corpus-wide even though Dahui is a prominent early source: later named Chan authors define and deploy it independently, so historical prominence does not justify a person-specific SenseKey. Hanyue also records the comparison, 'In ancestral-teacher Chan it is called the saying; among Confucians it is called investigating things' (在祖師禪謂之話頭，在儒家謂之格物). Tiemei's record asks separately about the head, tail, and waist of a saying (話頭、話尾、話腰). The corpus has only two hits for 'saying-tail' (話尾) and one for 'saying-waist' (話腰), so those forms are recorded as wordplay rather than general definitions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 只就動止處。看箇話頭。便是釋迦老子達磨大師出來也。只是這箇。僧問趙州。狗子還有佛性也無。州云無。

Occurrences.Kwic: 直至宋朝，始有看話頭、作工夫之說。當時只教人提起箇話頭，看是什麼道理？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Record of Chan Master Weilin Daopei's Return to the Mountain (為霖道霈禪師還山錄), in Weilin Daopei's winter-restriction general address to the assembly. Weilin Daopei is the exact speaker who says that only in the Song did talk of ‘looking at the saying’ and ‘doing the work’ arise, then describes people being told to raise a saying and look at its principle; Dahui Zonggao is discussed immediately afterward, not the speaker of this retrospective.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Discourse on Forging in the Chan Gate (禪門鍛鍊說). Jiexian calls guarding a dead saying without raising doubt a serious illness of Chan investigation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：「如何是話頭？」師云：「腳上生腳。」「如何是話尾？」師云：「如牛無角。」「如何是話腰？」師云：「你且行路。」

Senses.PreferredTarget: a saying, remark, or turn in an exchange
Senses.Explanation: In encounter records, the same word denotes words spoken in an exchange: a saying, a remark, or the turn being carried by the speakers. Dongshan Liangjie appraises one as “a fine saying; it only lacks a follow-up line” (好箇話頭，只欠進語). Yunmen Xianqin speaks after a long silence and calls it “a fine saying” (好箇話頭), adding that it must not be recited wrongly elsewhere. Yunmen Wenyan asks for “my saying” to be returned (還我話頭來). In the “three pounds of hemp” exchange, Fuyan Liangya says that Dongshan Shouchu supposed Liangya did not understand “his saying” (他這話頭), referring to Dongshan’s answer. Recurrent forms confirm the deployment: “return my saying,” 78 hits in 44 texts; “does not even recognize the saying,” 185 hits in 87 texts; “remember the saying,” 68 hits in 61 texts; and “a fine saying,” 24 hits in 21 texts. The records do not assign one further gloss to all of these conversational uses.
Senses.Note: This sense covers a unit within recorded speech rather than a specified word, question, or saying that someone is told to investigate. It remains lexically connected to the first sense; the split records the distinct constructions and deployments rather than positing two unrelated words.

Occurrences.Kwic: 洞山，山云：好箇話頭，只欠進語。曹云：進甚麼語？洞云：何不問？為甚麼不道？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Linked Lamps Compendium (聯燈會要). Dongshan Liangjie calls the remark 'a fine saying' and says it lacks only a follow-up line; the passage then records the requested follow-up.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。一口吞盡時如何。師曰。我在你肚裏。曰。和尚為甚麼在學人肚裏。師曰。還我話頭來。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps Compendium (五燈會元), in Yunmen Wenyan's section. In a direct exchange, Yunmen answers the follow-up with 'Return my saying to me.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。良久曰。好箇話頭。若到諸方。不得錯舉。便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps Compendium (五燈會元), in Yunmen Wenyan's section. Yunmen calls the words just spoken 'a fine saying' and warns the assembly not to repeat them wrongly elsewhere.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧出問。如何是佛。山答曰。麻三斤。參罷。山至寮謂師曰。我今日答這僧話。得麼。曰。恰值某淨髮。山曰。你元來作這去就。拂袖便出。師曰。這老漢將謂我明他這話頭不得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps Compendium (五燈會元), in Fuyan Liangya's section. Fuyan says Dongshan Shouchu thought that Fuyan did not understand Dongshan's remark.
